title: Connector Saga: streaming primitives and lazy-resolve SDK ergonomics (PRD sketch)
content:
Purpose
This is a sketch PRD for an SDK and server contract that enables: streaming responses, multi-step connector/tool call sagas, and a lightweight "lazy-resolve" handshake for structured outputs. The focus is ergonomics for JS/TS and Python clients and predictable server-side fallback behavior when connectors fail or time out.

Context and motivation
- We have many internal PRDs on streaming framing, typed outputs, and partial responses. This doc tries to unify an ergonomics-first SDK surface for connector-heavy flows (think search + db + external api calls) where the model emits a plan that results in multiple tool invocations.
- Primary problem: developers currently wire tool calls ad-hoc in SDKs which leads to brittle error handling, duplicated retry logic, and poor UX for incremental UI updates.
- Secondary: we want clear server-side semantics so hosted API can gracefully degrade to safe textual fallback when connectors fail, without forcing app teams to rework control flow.

Goals (product-level)
1) Provide streaming primitives that deliver partial model text and discrete tool-call frames with clear ordering guarantees.
2) Offer a typed "lazy-resolve" contract so clients can display tentative structured results immediately and patch them when connectors return authoritative values.
3) Make SDK ergonomics minimal: few primitives, clearly documented lifecycles, small bundle size for frontend SDKs.
4) Define server fallback rules so Hosted API SLA and billing semantics remain straightforward.
5) Allow observability: per-call telemetry for token-latency, connector duration, and failover reason.

Non-goals
- This is not a full protocol PRD for every streaming use case (e.g., large file upload streaming).
- We are not solving advanced distributed transaction semantics between connector calls (no two-phase commit).

User stories
- Frontend dev: I want to show a conversation transcript with inline results (e.g., search snippets) as soon as the model requests them, and then replace them when the external search completes.
- Backend dev: I want a single handler that receives tool-call events and can decide to run them locally or queue them to an async worker, and still keep the client session consistent.
- Integrations engineer: I want predictable retry semantics and simple error codes to map into customer-facing messages.

Concepts and vocabulary (short)
- stream-frame: a single unit in the streaming API (text chunk | tool-invoke | tool-result | checkpoint).
- toollet: a lightweight connector invocation (could be sync HTTP call, DB query, or async job).
- saga: ordered sequence of toollets invoked as part of a single model response.
- lazy-resolve token: a short id representing a value the model expects to be filled in by a connector; client can render placeholder object.

High-level flow
1) Client initiates a streaming call (POST /v1/streams).
2) Server streams text frames and tool-invoke frames as model emits them. Tool-invoke frames include a tool id, params, and a suggested mode (sync/async).
3) Hosted runtime either calls the connector (if configured) or forwards the tool-invoke frame to the customer's function endpoint (webhook / message queue) depending on policy.
4) Server emits one of: tool-result frame (when connector returns), tool-fallback frame (when connector fails or times out), or tool-deferred frame (acknowledging async handling with lazy-resolve key).
5) When lazy-resolve key resolves, server emits a patch frame referencing the key and providing authoritative structured content.

Streaming frame contract (sketch)
- text_chunk: { type: "text_chunk", seq: int, text: string }
- tool_invoke: { type: "tool_invoke", seq: int, tool: string, params: json-serializable, mode: "sync"|"async"|"deferred", suggested_ttl_ms?: int }
- tool_result: { type: "tool_result", seq: int, tool: string, result: json-serializable, status: "ok"|"error"|"partial" }
- tool_fallback: { type: "tool_fallback", seq: int, tool: string, reason: string, fallback_text?: string }
- lazy_resolve_ack: { type: "lazy_resolve_ack", seq: int, key: string, expires_at: iso_ts }
- patch: { type: "patch", seq: int, key: string, payload: json-serializable }
(note: actual wire format is newline-delimited JSON frames)

Server policies (defaults)
- sync mode: server will attempt connector call inline for up to 1s by default. If connector completes in that window, emit tool_result inline.
- deferred mode: server will acknowledge immediately with lazy_resolve_ack and schedule connector (or forward). Server must emit either a patch or a tool_fallback within TTL (default 30s) or emit a final tool_fallback indicating timeout.
- async mode: server may stream tool_result later in the same connection if it stays open; otherwise client must subscribe to a session endpoint or receive a webhook.
- fallback rules: on connector error, server emits tool_fallback with reason mapping to standardized error codes (TIMEOUT, UNREACHABLE, AUTH_ERROR, RATE_LIMIT, INTERNAL). fallback_text is recommended human readable suggestion for clients to surface.

Lazy-resolve contract rationale
- Many apps want the UX of immediate structured data (e.g., a table of search results) but connectors can be slow. Lazy-resolve provides an id that the model can reference, letting clients render a lightweight interactive placeholder while authoritative data is fetched. This makes optimistic UIs easier and avoids blocking streaming text.

SDK ergonomics (JS/TS & Python)
Design principles
- Minimal primitives: stream(), onFrame(cb), cancel(). Keep connector wiring outside of stream() surface.
- Declarative handling: provide helpers to automatically render patches into a structured object given a schema.
- Low cognitive load: standard error mapping, default retry heuristics, and clear lifecycle events.

JS pseudocode (client)
const s = client.stream({ model: 'r-infer-medium', prompt: 'Find latest docs about X' })
s.onFrame(frame => {
  switch(frame.type) {
    case 'text_chunk': appendText(frame.text); break;
    case 'tool_invoke': showToolPlaceholder(frame.seq, frame.tool, frame.params); if (frame.mode === 'sync') { /* nothing: server will return inline */ } else if (frame.mode === 'deferred') { registerLazyKey(frame.key); } break;
    case 'patch': applyPatch(frame.key, frame.payload); break;
    case 'tool_fallback': showFallback(frame.tool, frame.reason, frame.fallback_text); break;
  }
});

Server-side handler options for integrations
- Inline adapter: Hosted API calls connector endpoint synchronously, returns result directly. Good for low-latency connectors.
- Queue adapter: Hosted API emits lazy_resolve_ack and enqueues job; connector worker picks up job and posts result to callback URL.
- Proxyable adapter: customer requests that all tool_invoke frames be forwarded to their proxy endpoint for authorization/logging before invoking connectors.

Telemetry and observability
- Emit trace/span per tool_invoke with: seq, tool, mode, start_ts, end_ts, duration_ms, status, fallback_reason.
- Per-session metrics: total_tool_calls, avg_tool_latency, percent_tool_fallback.
- Add a debug flag to stream request to capture full frame log for 7 days (opt-in).

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Ordering guarantees: do we guarantee strict seq ordering for patches relative to text? Proposed: seq is monotonic per-session; clients should apply frames in seq order. But we may allow out-of-order delivery for performance — need to evaluate complexity.
- TTL and billing: deferred flows may incur queue processing cost; should customers be billed for lifetime of pending lazy keys? Proposal: bill for when tool_result is delivered (consumed tokens) + fixed per-toollet overhead.
- Security: proxyable adapter increases surface for data exfiltration; we need per-tool RBAC and audit logs.
- SDK size: we should keep default browser bundle < 15KB gzipped beyond network library. That limits heavy schema validation libraries; provide opt-in helpers.

Migration and rollout plan (high level)
1) Implement frame types on v1/streams experimental endpoint and a simple JS SDK wrapper (beta) that exposes onFrame.
2) Pilot with Solutions team + 2 customers integrating a search connector via deferred mode.
3) Add telemetry and admin dashboard to view saga traces.
4) Iterate on error code taxonomy and TTL defaults.

Risks and mitigations
- Complexity for app devs: mitigate with clear examples, SDK helpers for common connector patterns, sample server adapters.
- Operational cost: deferred jobs can pile up; set sane quota / TTL defaults and implement queue pruning.
- UX noise: partial placeholders might cause flicker. Provide client guidance on placeholders and patch animations in the developer playbook.

Next steps (near-term tasks)
- Design meeting with infra/serving-runtime to validate seq monotonicity and routing implications (Ravi).
- Prototype JS SDK streaming client + small demo app (June).
- Draft connector error-code mapping and attach to logging schema (Liam).
- Prepare pilot checklist for customers including security review and quota settings (Marisol).

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally sketch-level. Looking for feedback on: seq ordering guarantees, TTL defaults (1s inline, 30s deferred by default), and default mode selection heuristics.
- Also want thoughts on whether to expose lazy-resolve keys in text output (e.g., the model writes "[result_23]" in the text) vs. keeping them only in frames.

Appendix: example session transcript (simplified)\CLIENT => POST /v1/streams { prompt: "Find top 3 docs about privacy law in EU" }
SERVER -> stream frames:
- text_chunk(seq=1, text="I found a few documents: ")
- tool_invoke(seq=2, tool="search_v1", params={q:"privacy law EU"}, mode="deferred", key="k_23")
- text_chunk(seq=3, text="I'll summarize them once I have results...")
- lazy_resolve_ack(seq=4, key="k_23", expires_at="2025-01-22T12:34:56Z")
(later)
- patch(seq=5, key="k_23", payload={items:[{title:"GDPR overview", url:"..."}, ...]})
- text_chunk(seq=6, text="Summary: ...")

End.
